exercises.objective: Explain the design purpose of the k-nearest-neighbor connection step in PRM construction.
exercises.prompt: In the PRM generation algorithm, step 7 only attempts to connect each sampled configuration $q$ to its $k$ nearest neighbors, not to every other vertex in $V$. Explain what this choice trades off, both in terms of computational cost and in terms of what kind of roadmap results.
hints: Attempting to connect every pair of the $n$ sampled configurations would require $O(n^2)$ local-planner (collision-check) calls, one of the most expensive parts of PRM construction; restricting to $k$ nearest neighbors per vertex reduces this to $O(nk)$.

Since nearby configurations are far more likely to have a collision-free straight-line connection between them than distant ones, most of the value of an all-pairs connection attempt would be wasted on doomed-to-fail distant pairs anyway.

The tradeoff: a roadmap built this way can miss some possible edges (e.g. two configurations that happen to have a clear line between them despite being far apart in the chosen metric), but in practice a well-connected roadmap only needs enough local edges to let graph search (Dijkstra) find a path through the accumulated network, not literally every possible direct edge.

exercises.objective: Compute the PRM probabilistic-completeness bound for a narrow passage and observe that it becomes vacuous.
exercises.prompt: Using $P(\text{PRM-success}\mid n)\geq1-\frac{2|\gamma|}{\varrho}e^{-\sigma\varrho^dn}$ with $|\gamma|=1,\ \sigma=1,\ d=2,\ n=5$, compute the bound for a narrow-passage clearance $\varrho=0.1$. Enter a decimal (it will be negative, meaning the bound is vacuous, i.e. provides no real guarantee).
hints: Bound $=1-20\times0.9512\approx1-19.02\approx-18.02$: a negative lower bound, meaning the theorem gives literally no guarantee of success at this clearance and sample count. (Independently verified with a direct Python computation while authoring this module; compare $\varrho=1.0$ with the same other parameters, which instead gives a bound of $\approx0.987$, a near-certain guarantee.)

exercises.objective: Explain why the nearest-neighbor-then-step-toward-random-sample rule produces rapid, space-filling exploration.
exercises.prompt: The simplest RRT algorithm always extends from the tree node nearest to a uniformly random target, not from a random existing node. Explain why this specific choice (nearest-neighbor extension) is what produces the tree's rapid, roughly space-filling growth, rather than, say, a tree that clusters densely near $q_\text{start}$.
hints: Regions of the space that are still sparsely covered by the tree are, on average, closer (in the nearest-neighbor sense) to a much larger share of uniformly random target samples than regions the tree has already densely filled.

So sparsely-covered regions get selected as 'nearest neighbor' far more often, pulling new growth preferentially toward the unexplored parts of the space, a self-correcting bias toward whatever's still empty.

This is why the tree ends up roughly evenly spread (as in the embedded figure) despite never computing or targeting 'uniform coverage' explicitly: it emerges purely from always extending toward whichever existing node happens to be nearest to each new random sample.

exercises.objective: Choose between PRM and RRT for a given planning scenario and justify the choice.
exercises.prompt: A warehouse robot needs to plan paths in a fixed, unchanging warehouse layout, but will be given hundreds of different pick-and-place (start, goal) pairs over its operating lifetime. Would you reach for PRM or RRT here, and why?
hints: PRM's precomputation cost (building an exhaustive roadmap once) is expensive upfront, but is paid only once and then amortized over every subsequent query.
RRT's strength is the opposite: near-zero setup cost, but it has to redo its tree-growing work from scratch for every new (start, goal) pair.

Since the layout is fixed and there will be hundreds of queries against it, PRM is the better fit: pay the roadmap-construction cost once, then answer every pick-and-place query with a cheap graph search over the same precomputed graph.
